title: Occasion and date
short: A comic dialogue, dated 'Westbourne Park Villas, 1866', between a country girl and her friend 'Melia, now a kept woman in London.
body: Hardy wrote the poem in 1866 while he was working in London as an assistant to the architect Arthur Blomfield and lodging at Westbourne Park Villas, Paddington; it was not published until Poems of the Past and the Present (1901). 'Melia is short for Amelia. A girl just up from the country meets her old companion in 'Town' (London) and marvels at her fine clothes; 'Melia explains each change by her 'ruin', the Victorian word for a woman's loss of chastity outside marriage. The poem turns the solemn literature of the 'fallen woman' (from Victorian sermons to Rossetti's 'Jenny') into satire: ruin has brought comfort, idleness and polish.

title: ruined
short: Seduced and 'fallen': the Victorian euphemism for a woman who has lost her virtue, here worn as a badge of prosperity.
body: In Victorian usage a 'ruined' woman was one seduced or living as a mistress, who had thereby, in respectable opinion, lost her prospects of marriage and her place in society; the OED records this sense of ruin from the eighteenth century. Hardy exploits the gap between the moral word and the material facts: the 'ruined' maid is the one whose life has visibly improved, while the virtuous girl is still in rags. The irony anticipates Hardy's later quarrel with conventional sexual morality in Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891), subtitled 'A Pure Woman'. 'Melia's replies keep returning to the word, as 'ruined' or 'ruin', in all six stanzas.

title: Wrenched rhymes: 'prosperi-ty', 'compa-ny'
short: Hyphenated words force an unnatural stress onto the last syllable so it can rhyme with 'she'.
body: The poem is in rhymed couplets of anapestic tetrameter (four strong beats, mostly with two light syllables between them: 'Who could HAVE sup-POSED I should MEET you in TOWN?'). The third line of each stanza ends on a polysyllable split by a hyphen, 'prosperi-ty', 'compa-ny', 'la-dy', 'melancho-ly', so that its final syllable takes a stress and rhymes with the refrain's 'she'. The wrenched stress is a ballad and music-hall effect, and it mimics the country speaker's awkward, over-careful pronunciation of the grand words she uses for her friend's new life. The jaunty metre itself undercuts any tragic reading of ruin.

title: spudding up docks
short: Digging up dock-weeds with a spud, a narrow spade or chisel-headed tool: the hard farm labour 'Melia has escaped.
body: A spud is a small, narrow-bladed spade or weeding chisel, and to 'spud' is to dig out weeds with it; docks are the broad-leaved weeds (Rumex) that infest pasture. The Victorian Web glosses the phrase as digging up weeds with a chisel-headed spade. Together with 'digging potatoes' and going 'without shoes or socks', the phrase sums up the life of a female field labourer in Dorset, the kind of work Tess does at Flintcomb-Ash in Hardy's novel. The contrast with 'gay bracelets and bright feathers three' is the poem's whole argument in miniature.

title: bright feathers three
short: Ostrich plumes on a fashionable hat, a sign of a woman of fashion (and, to the knowing reader, of a kept woman).
body: Large ostrich feathers on a hat or bonnet were high fashion for women in the 1860s; three plumes was a lavish display. The detail, like the bracelets, the 'fair garments' and the 'little gloves', belongs to the dress of a lady, but on a former farm girl it would be read by any worldly observer as the sign of a mistress maintained by a wealthy man. The innocent speaker reads the signs literally and envies them, and in the last stanza she wishes for 'feathers, a fine sweeping gown'. 'Melia's reply, 'that's how we dress when we're ruined', is a knowing joke at the expense of moral language.

title: barton
short: Dorset dialect for a farmyard, or the farm buildings and yard together.
body: From Old English beretun ('barley enclosure', i.e. threshing-floor or grange), a barton in south-western dialect is a farmyard or the home farm of an estate. Barnes's Dorset glossary and the Victorian Web both gloss it as farmyard or barn. Hardy uses the word throughout the Wessex novels (for instance in Far from the Madding Crowd). It fixes 'Melia's origins in the working farm.

title: 'thee' and 'thou', 'thik oon', 'the's oon', 't'other'
short: Dorset dialect forms, 'that one', 'this one', 'the other', which 'Melia has dropped for polite London English.
body: In the Dorset dialect recorded by Hardy's friend William Barnes, 'thik' means 'that' (so 'thik oon' is 'that one'), the form printed here as 'the’s oon' (Hardy's 'theäs oon', garbled in the archive text) represents 'this one', and 't'other' is 'the other'. Rural speakers also kept the old familiar pronouns 'thee' and 'thou', long gone from polite speech. The country girl notes that 'Melia now talks in a way that fits 'ee (you) for high company; the joke is that her own phrasing ('fits 'ee') is itself dialect. Speech marks class, and ruin has given 'Melia the accent of a lady.

title: hands like paws, face blue and bleak
short: The marks of outdoor work in winter: rough, swollen hands and a face blue with cold.
body: The country girl's memories are blunt and physical. Field work in the cold left hands red, chapped and clumsy, 'like paws', and faces 'blue and bleak' (pinched with cold). Against this she sets 'Melia's 'delicate cheek' and gloves that fit as on any lady. The point, made with comic exaggeration, is economic: the respectable life available to a poor rural woman was hard manual labour, and the 'fallen' life offered comfort. 'Melia's reply, 'We never do work when we're ruined', states the bargain plainly.

title: hag-ridden dream
short: A nightmare; folk belief held that a hag or witch rode on sleepers' chests, causing bad dreams.
body: To be 'hag-ridden' was originally to be ridden by a hag or witch in one's sleep, the folk explanation of nightmare (the 'mare' of nightmare is a goblin that sits on the sleeper). By extension the word means oppressed or harassed. 'Melia once called home life a 'hag-ridden dream', a waking nightmare of drudgery. Hardy, a collector of Dorset superstitions, uses such beliefs throughout his fiction.

title: sock; megrims
short: To 'sock' is Dorset for to sigh heavily; 'megrims' are low spirits or migraines.
body: Barnes's Dorset glossary defines 'sock' as to sigh with a loudish sound. 'Megrims', from French migraine and ultimately Greek hemikrania ('half the head'), meant a one-sided headache and then, figuratively, low spirits or whims, and Victorian Web notes gloss it along these lines. The country girl recalls 'Melia sighing and moping at home, and now sees in her no trace of 'melancho-ly'. 'Melia agrees: 'There's an advantage in ruin.'

title: Refrain: '... said she'
short: Each stanza ends with 'Melia's reply and the tag 'said she', a ballad-like refrain that varies the word 'ruin'.
body: The poem is built as a dialogue in which the country girl speaks three lines and 'Melia answers in the fourth, always closing with 'said she'. The refrain gives the poem the shape of a folk ballad or music-hall song, and the variation within it ('ruined', 'ruin', 'ruin', 'ruined') creates the comedy of repetition. 'Melia's answers grow more knowing as the poem goes on, from surprise ('O didn't you know') to a frank statement of advantage.

title: 'You ain't ruined'
short: 'Melia's polish cracks: her final retort lapses into dialect ('such as you be', 'ain't'), exposing the veneer.
body: In the last stanza the country girl wishes for 'Melia's finery and the freedom to 'strut about Town'. 'Melia's answer is condescending, a raw country girl 'isn't equal to that', but its grammar betrays her: 'such as you be' and 'You ain't ruined' are rustic, not ladylike. Critics read the slip in different ways: as a final comic deflation of 'Melia's pretensions; as a hint that the 'polish' gained with ruin is thin and her position precarious; or as a sign that the two women remain sisters under the skin. The poem refuses to moralise either way, and Hardy leaves the reader to weigh the costs of 'ruin' that 'Melia never mentions.
